docs.title: General
docs.text: Key Type Default Description app_name str "Pipeline creator" Title displayed in the OS viewport title bar. ui_scale_multiplier float 0.75 Global scale multiplier applied on top of DPI auto-scaling. Adjust to enlarge or shrink UI elements across displays. preload_modules bool true If true, preloads and caches all module classes at startup (instant instantiation, slightly longer initial startup). If false, modules load on first instantiation. skip_import_validation bool false If true, skips startup module import health checks for faster boot. Manual health checks from Tools → Health Check remain available.

docs.title: Splash
docs.text:
Controls the animated splash screen shown while the application initializes.

Key Type Default Description enabled bool true Show or hide the splash screen on startup. image str "ressources/tutorial_assets/tutorial/Tutorial3.png" Relative path to the splash image file. size int 400 Width and height of the splash window in pixels. thickness int 2 Border thickness of the animated splash progress ring.

docs.title: Icon
docs.text: Key Type Default Description path str "ressources/icon.ico" Relative path to the application window icon (.ico).

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
Controls the login and profile selection prompt at startup.

Key Type Default Description enabled bool false If true, requests profile selection before opening the main window. default_mode str "dev" Pre-selected privilege mode: "user", "advanced", or "dev".

Deploying to operators

Set enabled: true and default_mode: "user" when deploying machines to operators. Non-developer accounts only see simplified, operator-safe controls.

docs.title: UI
docs.text: Key Type Default Description theme_name str "DEFAULT" Name of the active color palette (must match a dictionary in config/theme_colors.py). colorblind_type str "none" Colorblind correction palette: "none", "universal", "protanopia", "deuteranopia", "tritanopia". mascot bool true Toggle display of the assistant mascot graphic in the main viewport. enable_highlight bool true Default activation state for downstream connection wire highlighting in the Node Editor.

docs.title: Debug
docs.text: Key Type Default Description enabled bool true Enable global debug flags and extended logging. log_level str "TRACE" Minimum log severity level ("TRACE", "DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR", "CRITICAL"). log_mkdocs bool false Redirect stdout/stderr from the embedded MkDocs server subprocess into the main log stream.

docs.title: Window
docs.text: Key Type Default Description vsync bool true Enable vertical sync in the DearPyGui rendering loop to prevent tearing. minimize_to_tray bool false Minimize the application to the system tray instead of the OS taskbar. tray_offscreen bool true Move the window offscreen before minimizing to tray to eliminate visual flickering. show_console bool true Show or hide the background terminal console on Windows.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text: Key Type Default Description working_directory str "experiments" Default root folder for loading and saving data, pipelines, and export files. default_pipeline str \| null null Path to a pipeline JSON file to load automatically on application launch. default_automation_script str \| null "" Path to an automation JSON script to execute automatically on launch. show_loader_on_startup bool true Show an interactive dialog at startup to choose a pipeline or script if none is specified. default_pipeline_folder str "pipelines" Default directory for saving and browsing pipeline flow files. default_scripts_folder str "scripts" Default directory for saving and browsing automation scripts.

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
Module-specific hardware configuration for industrial cameras:

Key Type Default Description IDS.rotation int 90 Video feed rotation angle in degrees (0, 90, 180, 270) for IDS camera modules. Alvium.rotation int 90 Video feed rotation angle in degrees (0, 90, 180, 270) for Allied Vision Alvium camera modules.

docs.title: Viewers
docs.text:
Configuration for high-throughput image and video rendering modules:

Key Type Default Description image_viewer.texture_mode str "raw" Texture upload mode: "raw" (direct GPU streaming for high-FPS feeds) or "static" (zero PCIe transfer when idle). image_viewer.preserve_aspect_ratio bool false Preserve image aspect ratio (true) or stretch pixels to fill the viewport (false). video_viewer.texture_mode str "static" Texture upload mode for video playback: "raw" or "static". video_viewer.preserve_aspect_ratio bool false Preserve video aspect ratio (true) or stretch to canvas (false).

docs.title: SequenceProcessor
docs.text:
Settings for automated sequence execution and optical triggers:

Key Type Default Description end_seq_cmd str \| list "R0G0B0W0IR1000" Command string or list of commands dispatched automatically to hardware upon sequence completion.

docs.title: Visual Configuration Editor
docs.text: All parameters in config.json can be inspected and edited through a dedicated visual window: - Open Tools → Config Editor from the top menu bar. - Descriptions, sliders, dropdown selectors, and file/folder browsers are automatically rendered based on metadata annotations in config/config_anotation.json. - Changes are applied immediately and written to config/config.json upon clicking Save.

docs.title: Accessing Config in Code
docs.text:
Use the config singleton (core.config_manager.config) anywhere across the codebase:

from core.config_manager import config

# Direct dictionary access
app_name = config.get("General", {}).get("app_name", "Pipeline Creator")

# Deeply nested helper access with fallback defaults
scale = config.get_nested("General", "ui_scale_multiplier", default=1.0)
rotation = config.get_nested("Cameras", "IDS", "rotation", default=0)

# Modify and persist changes programmatically
config["UI"]["theme_name"] = "OCEAN_DARK"
config.save()

docs.title: Core vs Dynamic Modules
docs.text: Pipeline Creator's codebase is cleanly divided into two layers: the static core framework that is never modified by users, and the dynamic module ecosystem where all project-specific work happens.

docs.title: The Two Layers at a Glance
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph Static["🏛️ Static Core (core/ & config/)"]
        W[WindowBase] 
        P[ProcessingBase]
        NE[NodeEditor]
        MR[ModuleRegistry]
        AS[AppState]
        LB[LinkBus]
        TM[ThemeManager]
        DS[DisplayScaling]
    end

    subgraph Dynamic["🧩 Dynamic Modules (modules/)"]
        M1[my_ui_module_win.py]
        M2[my_processor.py]
        M3[custom_code.py]
    end

    M1 -- "inherits from" --> W
    M2 -- "inherits from" --> P

docs.title: Static Core (core/ and config/)
docs.text: The static core is the framework. You should never need to modify these files unless you are changing fundamental application behavior.

docs.title: Core Services
docs.text: File Purpose core/window_base.py Base class for all visual UI node modules core/processing_base.py Base class for background multiprocess workers core/node_editor.py Visual graph canvas, link handling, minimap core/module_registry.py Module discovery, loading, validation, serialization core/app_state.py Global session state singleton core/link_bus.py Publish/subscribe zero-wire data broker core/node_highlight.py Downstream graph highlighting & dimming core/node_popup.py Right-click module search popup core/node_callbacks.py DPG mouse event & link event handling core/node_serialization.py Flow JSON save/load & graph reconstruction core/login_dialog.py Login/profile dialog at startup core/main_win.py Main window menu bar & host container core/fusion_manager.py Tab-docking for module panel fusion core/dependency_manager.py Missing package detection & reporting core/module_validation_manager.py Post-load module contract enforcement core/automation_manager.py JSON script-driven startup automation core/input_output_types.py IOTypes enum for typed terminal connections core/tutorial_manager.py In-app guided tutorial system core/system_tray.py System tray icon & context menu core/splash.py Isolated splash screen process core/paths.py Centralized project path constants

docs.title: Config Layer
docs.text: File Purpose config/config.json User-editable application settings config/config.py Safe JSON loader with defaults config/theme_manager.py Theme/palette loading & font management config/theme_colors.py All color palette dictionaries config/theme_factory.py DPG theme item builders config/display_scaling.py DPI detection & multi-monitor scaling

docs.title: Dynamic Modules (modules/)
docs.text: The dynamic module layer is where you do all your project-specific work. Modules are Python files placed anywhere inside the /modules directory tree.

docs.title: Module Types
docs.text: Type Base Class Use Case UI Node WindowBase Interactive panels, charts, controls, viewers Processor ProcessingBase CPU-bound background computation Hybrid WindowBase + embedded ProcessingBase A UI panel that owns a background worker

docs.title: Discovery Contract
docs.text:
For the registry to discover your module, the file must expose:

# At module level (not inside a class or function)
EXPORTED_CLASS = MyModuleClass   # The class to instantiate
EXPORTED_NAME  = "My Module"     # Display name in the search popup

Optionally, a category can be specified. If not, the folder name is used as the category.

docs.title: Module Isolation Guarantee
docs.text:
Each module instance is completely isolated:

  • Its own UUID prevents DPG tag collisions.
  • Its own subprocess (if using ProcessingBase) prevents GIL interference.
  • Its own close() method ensures cleanup on shutdown.

docs.title: Base Classes: WindowBase vs ProcessingBase
docs.text: All dynamic modules in Pipeline Creator inherit from one of two core base classes defined in the static framework. These classes determine the execution context, thread safety, and responsibilities of the module.

docs.title: Core Differences
docs.text: Feature WindowBase ProcessingBase Primary Purpose Front-end GUI rendering, interactive charts, and user controls Background computation, CPU-bound processing, and hardware polling Execution Thread Runs in the Main Thread (GUI Thread) Runs in an isolated Subprocess (to bypass Python's GIL) Direct DPG Access Yes (can draw widgets, windows, handle UI events) No (attempting to call dearpygui functions will fail/crash) Blocking Safety Non-safe (long-running loops will freeze the entire UI) Safe (operates asynchronously without affecting GUI responsiveness) Communication Direct callbacks Thread-safe multiprocessing Queues (IPC)

docs.title: Communication Flows
docs.text: There are two primary ways modules interact within Pipeline Creator, depending on whether the communication occurs between different UI modules or internally between a UI node and its background worker.

docs.title: 1. Module-to-Module Communication (Direct Callbacks)
docs.text:
When you connect two nodes on the visual graph canvas, data is transmitted synchronously on the main thread using direct callbacks. For a deeper look at defining input callbacks and output connections, refer to the UI Node Developer Guide. 1. The target module (Module B) is registered inside the source module's (Module A) self.connections[output_name] dictionary. 2. When Module A generates new data, it loops over all registered target modules and calls their input_cb() method directly. 3. Module B receives the data via input_cb(data, data_type), updates its internal state, and refreshes its GUI widgets.

graph LR
    subgraph ModA["🧩 Module A - Source"]
        A_Logic["Internal Logic - DPG Callback"]
        A_Conn["self.connections.Output_Key"]
        A_Logic --> A_Conn
    end

    subgraph ModB["🧩 Module B - Target"]
        B_CB["input_cb method"]
        B_UI["Update UI Widgets - Render"]
        B_CB --> B_UI
    end

    A_Conn -->|direct callback call| B_CB

docs.title: 2. Hybrid Modules (Asynchronous IPC)
docs.text:
A Hybrid Module consists of a visual WindowBase layer running in the main thread (GUI) that instantiates and manages an isolated background ProcessingBase worker (Subprocess). This allows creating responsive nodes (like video players or real-time trackers) where user controls configure parameters dynamically while a background process handles the high-frequency calculation frame-by-frame. For advanced details on background process loops, queues, and subprocess lifecycle, see the Background Processor Developer Guide.

The WindowBase UI layer and the ProcessingBase worker communicate asynchronously using thread-safe Inter-Process Communication (IPC) queues: 1. The WindowBase UI component pushes raw data or parameters into the Input Queue. 2. The background ProcessingBase worker pulls the data from the queue, performs calculations, and pushes the results into the Output Queue. 3. The WindowBase UI component pulls the processed results from the Output Queue and updates the GUI widgets.

graph LR
    subgraph UI["🏛️ Module"]
        WB["UI Component - GUI"]
    end

    subgraph IPC["🔄 IPC Queues"]
        IQ["Input Queue"] ~~~ OQ["Output Queue"]
    end

    subgraph Worker["⚙️ ProcessingBase Layer - Background Process"]
        PB["Background Worker - GIL-free"]
    end

    WB -->|1. Push raw data| IQ
    IQ --> PB
    PB -->|2. Compute and Process| PB
    PB -->|3. Push results| OQ
    OQ --> WB

Developer Documentation

For detailed guidelines on how to subclass these base classes, check the following resources: - Developer Guide - Creating a UI Node with WindowBase - Creating a Processor with ProcessingBase

docs.title: Separation Rules
docs.text:
Action Where? Add a new visualization panel modules/your_category/name_win.py Add a new background processor modules/your_category/name_proc.py Change how modules are discovered core/module_registry.py Add a new color theme config/theme_colors.py Add a new menu item to the main bar core/main_win.py Change how link types are validated core/input_output_types.py Add a new IOType core/input_output_types.py → IOTypes enum

Never modify core files for project-specific logic

Project-specific logic should always live in modules/. Modifying core files risks breaking the framework for all other modules. If you find yourself needing a core change, consider whether the module can use input_cb, the link_bus, or a custom callback instead.

docs.title: Compiling & Distributing the Application
docs.text: Pipeline Creator provides a build script, make_executable.py that automates packaging the entire application into a standalone, portable folder. This compiled build contains the main executable (Pipeline_Creator.exe) along with the Python runtime and all required library dependencies.

docs.title: Why Compile to an Executable?
docs.text:
• Zero-Dependency Deployment: Users do not need to install Python, configure virtual environments, or run pip install commands. Everything runs out of the box.
  • Improved Performance & Protection: Compiles code using Nuitka, which translates Python code into highly optimized C++ source code before compile time.
  • Easy Distribution: The output main.dist directory can be easily compressed and shared.

docs.title: Compilation Settings (make_executable.py)
docs.text:
At the top of make_executable.py you can control the compilation behavior using the following variables:

# Path to a specific pipeline JSON, or None to compile everything
MAIN_PIPELINE = "pipelines/Webcam.json"  

# Output destination directory for Nuitka
OUTPUT_DIR = "C:/Users/demo/Desktop/Pipeline_creator"

docs.title: 1. Full Build (Compile All Modules)
docs.text:
To compile all modules and their dependencies:

  • Set MAIN_PIPELINE = None.
  • The script scans the entire modules/ directory, extracts all imported packages, and instructs Nuitka to include every single dependency in the bundle.
  • Best for: Internal developer builds or general-purpose pipeline creation environments.

docs.title: 2. Targeted Build (Compile Specific Pipeline)
docs.text:
To compile a lightweight bundle for a specific, final application:

  • Set MAIN_PIPELINE = "pipelines/YourPipeline.json".
  • The build script parses the JSON pipeline file to find only the modules referenced in that pipeline.
  • It dynamically computes the imports and dependency libraries of just those modules and excludes unused packages.
  • During the final stage, only the used module subfolders are copied to the main.dist/modules/ directory.
  • Best for: Shipping a locked, lightweight final product to end users.

docs.title: Running the Build
docs.text:
1. Ensure Nuitka and a compatible C compiler (like MSVC on Windows) are installed in your environment.
  2. Run the script from the terminal: 
    python make_executable.py
  3. Locate the output directory (specified by OUTPUT_DIR). The portable bundle is generated under <OUTPUT_DIR>/main.dist/.

docs.title: Creating a Background Processor (ProcessingBase)
docs.text: If your module performs CPU-intensive work (image processing, mathematical transforms, file scanning, serial communication loops), you must offload it to an isolated background process using ProcessingBase. This keeps the DPG render loop smooth and the UI frame rate stable.

docs.title: Why a Separate Process?
docs.text:
Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) means that threads cannot truly run Python code in parallel. A heavy computation in a thread will still stall the UI thread.

ProcessingBase uses multiprocessing, which spawns a separate OS process with its own Python interpreter and memory space, completely bypassing the GIL.

graph LR
    subgraph UI_Process["UI Process (main)"]
        DPG[DearPyGui Loop]
        Module[Your WindowBase Module]
    end
    subgraph Worker["Worker Process (isolated)"]
        PB[ProcessingBase Worker Loop]
        PD[_process_data method]
    end

    Module -- "submit(data)" --> InQ[("_in_queue")]
    InQ --> PB
    PB --> PD
    PD --> OutQ[("_out_queue")]
    OutQ -- "poll_result()" --> Module

    Module -- "update_params()" --> CtrlQ[("_ctrl_queue")]
    CtrlQ --> PB

docs.title: File Location
docs.text:
modules/<your_category>/<your_module_name>_proc.py

Convention: suffix the filename with _proc to indicate it is a background worker.

Note

A processor is not a standalone module, it is meant to be embedded inside a UI node (WindowBase subclass) that manages the process lifecycle.

docs.title: Minimal Template
docs.text:
This template corresponds to template_and_doc/processor_template.py:

from __future__ import annotations

import time
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional

from core.processing_base import ProcessingBase


class Processor_Template(ProcessingBase):
    """
    A template for building multiprocessing background worker processes.
    """

    # 1. Process Configuration (Class defaults - can also be overridden via kwargs)
    buffer_size = 10
    drop_policy = "drop_new"  # Options: 'drop_new', 'drop_oldest', or 'block'
    daemon = True

    def __init__(self, params: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """
        Initialize the processor process.

        Args:
            params: Optional initial parameters dictionary passed to the worker.
            **kwargs: Extra configuration options forwarded to ProcessingBase.
        """
        super().__init__(params=params, **kwargs)

    def _process_data(self, data: Any, params: Dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
        """
        Actual data processing logic executed in the isolated worker process.

        WARNING: This method runs in a different process.
        - Do NOT access DPG (dpg.*) from here.
        - Do NOT modify shared module state directly.
        - Only communicate via the return value (sent to out_queue).

        Args:
            data: The incoming data packet from the submission queue.
            params: Dictionary containing current parameters/configuration.

        Returns:
            The processed result to be pushed to the out_queue.
        """
        # Simulated workload
        time.sleep(1.0)

        # Example processing using data and params:
        factor = params.get("multiplier", 1)
        if isinstance(data, (int, float)):
            return data * factor

        return True

docs.title: Starting and Stopping
docs.text:
processor = Processor_Template(params={"multiplier": 2.0})
processor.start()    # Launch the background process
# ... later ...
processor.stop()     # Terminate gracefully

docs.title: Submitting Data
docs.text:
success = processor.submit(my_data)

submit() attempts to enqueue data for processing and returns True if accepted, or False if dropped/rejected. Behavior on saturation depends on the drop_policy:

Policy Behavior Implementation Details "drop_new" (default) Discard newly arriving item Fast producer-side check; leaves existing queue intact. "drop_oldest" Discard oldest item ("latest wins") Managed on the worker side via a dedicated receiver thread. The main process never unpickles discarded frames. "block" Block until space is available Blocks the calling thread until an input slot is free.

You can dynamically change the drop policy at runtime without restarting the process: 

processor.set_drop_policy("drop_oldest")

docs.title: Transparent Shared-Memory Transport
docs.text:
When working with heavy numerical payloads (such as large NumPy images, depth maps, or raw matrices), ProcessingBase automatically passes them through reusable shared memory pools (ShmPool via core/shm_transport.py) instead of serializing them through standard IPC pipes.

  • Zero-Copy: Massive arrays bypass Python pickle, avoiding GC pressure and frame copy delays.
  • Transparent: Subclasses send and return ordinary NumPy arrays without special encoding code.
  • Tunables (Class Attributes):
  • use_shared_memory: bool = True
  • shm_threshold_bytes: int = 64 * 1024 (Arrays smaller than 64 KB use the fast pickle path)
  • shm_max_pool_bytes: int = 512 * 1024 * 1024 (Cap per direction before fallback)

docs.title: Polling Results
docs.text:
result = processor.poll_result(timeout=None)
  • When timeout=None or <= 0: Non-blocking call returning immediately (None if queue is empty).
  • When timeout > 0: Blocks up to timeout seconds, releasing the Python GIL to avoid busy-wait spinlocks.
  • processor.get() and processor.get_results() are aliases of poll_result().

docs.title: Diagnostics & Monitoring
docs.text:
ProcessingBase provides built-in metrics used by the system profiler and Flow Metrics Viewer:

  • processor.is_ready() -> bool: Returns True if the worker is alive and queues are not full.
  • processor.has_data() -> bool: Returns True if a processed result is waiting in the output queue.
  • processor.queue_size() -> int: Returns the total number of pending items across IPC queue and worker buffer.
  • processor.drop_count() -> int: Total number of frames discarded by the worker under drop_oldest.
  • processor.clear(): Safely drains and releases all pending items in queues.

docs.title: Updating Parameters
docs.text:
processor.update_params({"multiplier": 3.5})

Parameters are sent to the worker via _ctrl_queue. The worker applies them before the next _process_data call without restarting the process.

docs.title: Integrating a Processor into a UI Node
docs.text:
The recommended pattern is a Hybrid module: a WindowBase subclass that owns and manages a ProcessingBase worker.

from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Any, Dict, Tuple, Optional
import dearpygui.dearpygui as dpg
from core.window_base import WindowBase
from core.input_output_types import IOTypes
from modules.processing.my_processor_proc import MyProcessor


class MyHybridNode(WindowBase):
    """
    A UI node with an embedded background processor.
    """

    def __init__(self, label="My Processor Node", ..., multiplier: float = 1.0) -> None:
        super().__init__(label=label, ...)

        self.persistent_fields = ["label", "multiplier"]
        self.accepted_input_types = [IOTypes.NUMBER]
        self.outputs = {"OUTPUT": IOTypes.NUMBER}
        self.connections = {k: [] for k in self.outputs}
        self.multiplier = multiplier

        # Create and start the background worker
        self._processor = MyProcessor(params={"multiplier": self.multiplier})
        self._processor.start()

        # ── DPG window using the self.window() context manager
        with self.window():
            dpg.add_text("Multiplier:")
            dpg.add_slider_float(
                tag=f"mult_slider_{self.UUID}",
                default_value=self.multiplier,
                min_value=0.1, max_value=10.0,
                callback=self._on_multiplier_changed,
            )

        # ── Register a DPG render callback to poll results each frame
        with dpg.item_handler_registry(tag=f"poll_handler_{self.UUID}"):
            dpg.add_item_visible_handler(callback=self._poll)
        dpg.bind_item_handler_registry(self.winID, f"poll_handler_{self.UUID}")

        self.update_permission()

    def _on_multiplier_changed(self, sender: Any, value: float) -> None:
        self.multiplier = value
        self._processor.update_params({"multiplier": value})

    def input_cb(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        data = kwargs.get("data") or (args[0] if args else None)
        if data is not None:
            self._processor.submit(data)

    def _poll(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Called each frame when the window is visible — polls for results."""
        result = self._processor.poll_result()
        if result and result.get("status") == "ok":
            from core.module_registry import MODULES_REGISTRY
            for uuid in self.connections.get("OUTPUT", []):
                target = MODULES_REGISTRY.get(uuid)
                if target:
                    target.input_cb(data=result["value"], data_type=IOTypes.NUMBER)

    def update_permission(self) -> None:
        from core.app_state import app_state
        is_user = (app_state.mode == "user")
        tag = f"mult_slider_{self.UUID}"
        if dpg.does_item_exist(tag):
            dpg.configure_item(tag, enabled=not is_user)

    def close(self) -> None:
        """Stop the background process on shutdown."""
        if hasattr(self, "_processor") and self._processor:
            self._processor.stop()
        super().close()


EXPORTED_CLASS = MyHybridNode
EXPORTED_NAME  = "My Processor Node"

docs.title: Important Constraints
docs.text:
No DPG access from the worker process

The _process_data method runs in a separate process — it has no access to DPG, the module registry, or any shared in-process state. All communication must go through the queues (submit / poll_result / update_params).

Serializable data only

Data passed through the queues must be picklable by Python's multiprocessing module. This includes: int, float, str, list, dict, numpy.ndarray. It excludes: DPG item IDs, open file handles, locks, and lambda functions.

docs.title: Programmatic Interface Prototyping
docs.text: While the standard workflow in Pipeline Creator is to build, prototype, or load layouts using the visual Node Editor, it is also possible to bypass the GUI canvas completely and instantiate and connect modules purely programmatically using Python.

docs.title: Standard Workflow vs. Programmatic Prototyping
docs.text:
1. Standard Workflow: Prototyping by adding nodes dynamically in the Node Editor, connecting terminals visually with wires, or loading pre-defined pipeline layouts (.json files) at startup or from the menu.
  2. Programmatic Prototyping: Writing a Python script that instantiates module classes as code, assigns their labels, dimensions, and window coordinates, and links them via programmatic connection methods.

docs.title: Programmatic Hello World Example
docs.text:
To connect a Hello World module to a Text Viewer module in code (mirroring what you would do in the visual Node Editor):

  1. Instantiate the module classes (HelloWorld_win and Text_viewer_win).
  2. Pass arguments like label, pos, win_width, and win_height.
  3. Call helloworld.connect_to(text_viewer, input_pin_index) to link them.

Here is the helper script from template_and_doc/manual_layout.py:

from modules.basic_ui.text_viewer_win import Text_viewer_win
from modules.basic_ui.Hello_world_win import HelloWorld_win

def create_windows() -> None:
    # 1. Instantiate modules with custom coordinates and labels
    helloworld = HelloWorld_win(label="Hello World", pos=(50, 50), win_width=300, win_height=200)
    text_viewer = Text_viewer_win(label="Text Viewer", pos=(350, 50), win_width=400, win_height=300)

    # 2. Programmatically connect output from helloworld to input index 0 of text_viewer
    helloworld.connect_to(text_viewer, 0)

docs.title: Loading a Programmatic Pipeline
docs.text:
To run your programmatic pipeline in the application, import and run it during startup. For example, in the initialization phase (e.g. inside main_win or main.py when preparing the UI):

from template_and_doc import manual_layout
manual_layout.create_windows()

This will instantiate the window items, set up their callbacks, draw the visual connection line in the background context, and render them on screen at launch.

docs.title: Exporting a Programmatically Built Pipeline
docs.text:
If you build a pipeline programmatically, you can serialize and save it directly to a pipeline JSON file so that it can be loaded later via the Node Editor. Call export_workspace from core.module_registry:

from core.module_registry import export_workspace

# Passing None as the first argument defaults to the global MODULES_REGISTRY
export_workspace(None, 'pipelines/manual_layout.json')

docs.title: Creating a Custom Theme
docs.text: Pipeline Creator's visual appearance is controlled by color palette dictionaries defined in config/theme_colors.py. Adding a new theme requires only adding a new dictionary, no code changes needed.

docs.title: How Themes Work
docs.text:
The ThemeManager auto-discovers all ALL_CAPS dictionaries in theme_colors.py at startup using:

for attr_name, palette in vars(theme_colors_module).items():
    if attr_name.isupper() and not attr_name.startswith("_"):
        if isinstance(palette, dict):
            PALETTES[attr_name] = palette

So a dictionary named DARK_OCEAN will automatically appear as the "DARK_OCEAN" theme in the Tools → Theme menu.

docs.title: Palette Dictionary Structure
docs.text:
A palette maps semantic color keys to RGBA tuples (R, G, B, A) where each channel is 0–255:

MY_THEME = {
    # Window chrome
    "window_bg":           (18, 18, 28, 255),
    "title_bar":           (30, 30, 50, 255),
    "title_bar_active":    (50, 50, 90, 255),
    "border":              (80, 80, 120, 200),

    # Buttons
    "button":              (60, 100, 180, 255),
    "button_hover":        (90, 130, 210, 255),
    "button_active":       (40,  80, 160, 255),

    # Text
    "text":                (220, 220, 230, 255),
    "text_disabled":       (120, 120, 140, 255),

    # Input fields
    "frame_bg":            (40,  40,  60, 255),
    "frame_bg_hover":      (55,  55,  80, 255),
    "frame_bg_active":     (70,  70, 100, 255),

    # Node editor
    "node_bg":             (30,  30,  50, 230),
    "node_border":         (80,  80, 130, 255),
    "node_title_bar":      (50,  50,  90, 255),
    "link_color":          (100, 200, 255, 255),

    # Highlights
    "highlight":           (255, 200,  50, 255),
    "error":               (220,  60,  60, 255),
    "success":             (60,  200, 100, 255),
}

docs.title: 1. Open config/theme_colors.py
docs.text:
Add your new palette dictionary at the bottom of the file:

# ── My Custom Dark Ocean Theme ─────────────────────────────────────────────
DARK_OCEAN = {
    "window_bg":        (10, 20, 40, 255),
    "title_bar":        (15, 35, 65, 255),
    "title_bar_active": (20, 50, 90, 255),
    "button":           (30, 100, 160, 255),
    "button_hover":     (50, 130, 190, 255),
    "text":             (200, 220, 240, 255),
    # ... add all required keys
}

docs.title: 2. Test It
docs.text: Restart Pipeline Creator and navigate to Tools → Theme → DARK_OCEAN. The palette applies immediately.

docs.title: 3. Persist It
docs.text:
To make your theme the default, update config.json:

"UI": {
    "theme_name": "DARK_OCEAN"
}

docs.title: Colorblind Variants
docs.text:
To provide a colorblind-safe version of your theme, suffix the palette name with the type:

DARK_OCEAN_DEUTERANOPIA = {
    # Same structure, adjusted colors for green-blind users
    "success": (50, 150, 255, 255),  # Blue instead of green
    ...
}

Set UI.colorblind_type to "deuteranopia" in config.json. The theme manager will automatically append the suffix and try to load the variant.

docs.title: Tips for Good Color Palettes
docs.text:
• Contrast ratio: Ensure text colors have at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio against their background for readability.
  • Node editor legibility: Node titles should be clearly distinct from the canvas background.
  • Use HSL thinking: Design your palette from a hue/saturation/lightness perspective, then convert to RGB. This makes it easy to create coherent light/dark variants.
  • Test with the log viewer open: The log viewer uses heavily styled text, it's a good stress-test for your palette.

docs.title: Managing Tutorials & Programmatic Hints
docs.text:
As a developer building new modules, you can integrate with Pipeline Creator's Tutorial Manager in two ways:

  1. Module-Specific Tutorials (tutorial.json): Auto-bind a pre-recorded walkthrough that users can trigger via the Node Editor.
  2. Programmatic API Invocations: Trigger real-time, context-aware highlights, errors, or alerts directly from your python module code.

You can programmatically trigger the Tutorial Manager to show hints, alerts, or enforce workflow rules based on live status or the current privilege mode (such as blocking a "user" action until they perform a prerequisite step):

from core.tutorial_manager import tutorial_manager
from core.app_state import app_state

# Example 1: Enforce a workflow rule in User Mode by blocking an action
# and automatically showing a tutorial reminder pointing to the required widget
def on_export_clicked(self):
    if app_state.mode == "user" and not self.sample_name:
        # Highlight the input field and display a helper alert
        tutorial_manager.play_error_hint(
            item_tag=self.sample_name_input_tag, 
            instruction="Workflow reminder: You must enter a Sample name/ID first."
        )
        return  # Block execution

    # Continue with action...

# Example 2: Highlight a widget with a success indicator
tutorial_manager.play_success_hint(
    item_tag=f"run_btn_{self.UUID}", 
    instruction="Calibration succeeded! Click here to start."
)

# Example 3: Display a central alert message on screen
tutorial_manager.play_center_hint(
    instruction="Connection lost. Reconnecting...", 
    type="error_hint", 
    icon_type="error"
)

docs.title: Creating a UI Node (WindowBase)
docs.text: Visual nodes inherit from WindowBase, which handles DPG window creation, UUID management, serialization, and connection event routing automatically.

docs.title: File Location
docs.text:
Create your module at: 

modules/<your_category>/<your_module_name>_win.py

Convention: suffix the filename with _win to indicate it is a visual node.

docs.title: Minimal Template
docs.text:
This template corresponds to template_and_doc/module_template.py:

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

import dearpygui.dearpygui as dpg
from loguru import logger

from core.input_output_types import IOTypes
from core.window_base import WindowBase


class Template_win(WindowBase):
    """
    A basic example module window using the WindowBase system.

    Demonstrates:
    - Declaring window defaults (label, win_width, win_height)
    - Declaring input/output types (checked by Module Health Check)
    - Saving persistent fields (e.g., default_number)
    - Handling incoming data via input_cb
    - Sending messages downstream to connected modules
    - Adapting UI permissions based on app_state mode
    """

    # 1. Window Configuration (Class defaults - can also be passed via kwargs)
    label = "Template"
    win_width = 300
    win_height = 200

    # 2. Input/Output definitions (Required by Module Health Check)
    accepted_input_types = [IOTypes.TEXT]
    outputs = {
        "TEXT": IOTypes.TEXT,
        "NUMBER": IOTypes.NUMBER,
    }

    # 3. Persistent fields saved into pipeline JSON
    persistent_fields = ["label", "default_number"]

    def __init__(self, default_number: int = 10, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

        self.default_number = default_number
        self.btn_tag = f"template_btn_{self.UUID}"
        self.number_tag = f"template_number_{self.UUID}"

        # Build DPG Window UI using the convenient self.window() context manager
        with self.window():
            dpg.add_button(tag=self.btn_tag, label="Hello world", callback=self.trigger_cb)

            dpg.add_input_int(
                tag=self.number_tag,
                default_value=self.default_number,
                callback=lambda sender, value: setattr(self, "default_number", value),
            )

        # Always refresh permissions after UI creation
        self.update_permission()

    def update_permission(self) -> None:
        """
        Adapts the module UI based on the application mode:
        - 'user'     : Restricted access (e.g., read-only fields, hidden buttons).
        - 'advanced' : Standard access.
        - 'dev'      : Full access to all internals.
        """
        from core.app_state import app_state

        mode = app_state.mode

        # Example 1: Hide an element in 'user' mode
        if dpg.does_item_exist(self.btn_tag):
            dpg.configure_item(self.btn_tag, show=(mode != "user"))

        # Example 2: Lock editing in 'user' mode
        if dpg.does_item_exist(self.number_tag):
            is_readonly = mode == "user"
            dpg.configure_item(self.number_tag, readonly=is_readonly, enabled=not is_readonly)

        # Example 3: Hide the entire window if needed (e.g., dev-only module)
        if mode == "user":
            dpg.hide_item(self.winID)

    def input_cb(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Processes incoming data from upstream connected nodes."""
        logger.debug(f"{self.winID} received input: args={args}, kwargs={kwargs}")

    def trigger_cb(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """Sends data downstream to connected modules."""
        for idx, output_key in enumerate(self.outputs):
            connected_modules = self.connections.get(output_key, [])
            for module in connected_modules:
                if idx == 0:
                    module.input_cb("Hello World")
                elif idx == 1:
                    module.input_cb(self.default_number)


EXPORTED_CLASS = Template_win
EXPORTED_NAME = "Template"

docs.title: WindowBase Contract
docs.text:
WindowBase.__init__() provides the following attributes that your module can use:

Attribute Type Description self.UUID str Unique identifier for this instance self.winID str DPG tag for the top-level window (f"{label}_{UUID}") self.label str Display name of the node self.pos tuple Current (x, y) position in pixels self.win_width int Window width in pixels self.win_height int Window height in pixels self.visible bool Whether the window is currently shown self.connections dict Maps output name → list of downstream UUIDs self.persistent_fields list Field names to save/restore in flow JSON self.accepted_input_types list IOTypes this node accepts as input self.outputs dict Maps output name → IOType

docs.title: Fusion (Tab-Docking) Support
docs.text:
If your node should support being "fused" into a FusionManager tab, WindowBase handles this automatically. The fusion manager will hide the standalone window and embed its children inside a tab panel.

No extra code is required, just ensure all your DPG children are created inside the with self.window(): context block.

docs.title: Node in the Node Editor (Graph Tab)
docs.text:
In addition to the floating window, each module instance is represented as a node card in the Node Editor canvas. This card shows: - The module label. - Colored input attribute terminals. - Colored output attribute terminals.

The node card is created automatically by the registry when your module is instantiated from the Node Editor popup. You do not need to create it manually.

docs.title: Testing Your Module
docs.text:
1. Place the file in modules/<category>/.
  2. Restart Pipeline Creator.
  3. Right-click the Node Editor canvas and search for your module name.
  4. Verify the node appears, the window opens, and the slider controls work.
  5. Connect an upstream node and verify input_cb is triggered.

docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the Pipeline Creator developer documentation. This guide covers everything you need to know to build new node modules — from a simple UI panel to a fully isolated background processor.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
All modules live inside the /modules directory, organized into category subdirectories:

modules/
├── basic_ui/
│   ├── csv_reader_win.py      ← UI node (WindowBase)
│   └── image_viewer_win.py
├── processing/
│   ├── signal_filter_proc.py  ← Processor (ProcessingBase)
│   └── data_normalizer_proc.py
└── my_category/
    └── my_new_module_win.py   ← Your new module goes here

Every module file needs to expose at module level:

EXPORTED_CLASS = MyModuleClass
EXPORTED_NAME  = "My Module Name"

The registry auto-discovers these at startup.

docs.title: Module Types
docs.text: Guide Description Creating a UI Node Build an interactive panel using WindowBase Creating a Processor Offload CPU work using ProcessingBase Creating a Theme Add a custom color palette

docs.title: Advanced Topics
docs.text: Guide Description Managing Tutorials Integrate step-by-step guides and workflow hints Programmatic Pipeline Construct pipelines and connect modules programmatically via code Compile Program Build standalone binaries using Nuitka

docs.title: 1. Always Suffix DPG Tags with self.UUID
docs.text:
DearPyGui maintains a global item registry. If two instances of the same module use identical string tags, DPG will crash with a duplicate ID error.

# ❌ Bad — crashes if two instances exist
dpg.add_button(tag="confirm_button")

# ✅ Good — UUID guarantees uniqueness
dpg.add_button(tag=f"confirm_button_{self.UUID}")

self.UUID is set automatically by WindowBase.__init__().

docs.title: 2. Implement update_permission()
docs.text:
This method is called automatically whenever the user switches privilege modes in the application. Pipeline Creator defines three standard user modes via core.app_state.app_state.mode:

  • "user": Operator mode. Restrict sensitive settings, lock calibration sliders, prevent window closure (no_close=True), and hide developer buttons.
  • "advanced": Power user / technician mode. Expose tuning parameters, offsets, and calibration controls.
  • "dev": Full developer access. Reveal raw debug buttons, internal inspectors, manual override triggers, and terminal output.

update_permission() allows you to dynamically adjust the operational freedom and complexity of your interface to match the user's role:

def update_permission(self) -> None:
    from core.app_state import app_state

    is_user = (app_state.mode == "user")
    is_dev = (app_state.mode == "dev")

    # 1. Prevent accidental window closure in operator mode
    if dpg.does_item_exist(self.winID):
        dpg.configure_item(self.winID, no_close=is_user)

    # 2. Lock or enable sensitive calibration controls
    if dpg.does_item_exist(self.calib_slider_tag):
        dpg.configure_item(self.calib_slider_tag, enabled=not is_user)

    # 3. Show or hide internal debugging panels
    if dpg.does_item_exist(self.debug_group_tag):
        (dpg.show_item if is_dev else dpg.hide_item)(self.debug_group_tag)

    # 4. Enforce safe default values when dropping to user mode
    if is_user and hasattr(self, "power_limit"):
        self.power_limit = min(self.power_limit, 50.0)

docs.title: 3. Declare persistent_fields
docs.text:
Fields listed in persistent_fields are automatically serialized into the flow JSON when the workspace is saved, and restored when the pipeline is reloaded.

Each string in the list must match an exact attribute name on self (self.attribute_name):

class MyFilterWin(WindowBase):
    label = "My Filter"

    # Declare class-level defaults
    threshold_val: float = 42.5
    default_path: str = "C:/data/records"
    enable_filter: bool = True

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

        # Attributes to serialize when saving the pipeline
        self.persistent_fields = ["label", "threshold_val", "default_path", "enable_filter"]

docs.title: How It Serializes in the Flow JSON
docs.text:
When the user saves the pipeline, WindowBase.to_dict() extracts every attribute listed in self.persistent_fields and places them into the "params" block of the module:

{
    "module": "my_category.my_filter_win",
    "class_name": "MyFilterWin",
    "uuid": "7a3f81e2-b94d-4819-a1b2-c0e812d34567",
    "pos": [140, 90],
    "size": [420, 280],
    "visible": true,
    "params": {
        "label": "My Filter",
        "threshold_val": 42.5,
        "default_path": "C:/data/records",
        "enable_filter": true
    }
}

When reloaded, WindowBase passes "params" as keyword arguments to __init__(**params) and automatically restores their values onto self.

docs.title: 4. Implement close() for Cleanup & Hardware Safety
docs.text:
The close() method is called automatically in three scenarios:

  1. Application Exit: When the program is closed.
  2. Node Deletion: When the user deletes the module or node from the canvas.
  3. Module Error / Crash: When an unhandled error triggers a safe teardown.

In your implementation:

  • Stop and join background threads or worker processes to prevent hanging or orphaned Python processes.
  • Send final safety shutdown commands to connected external devices: If your module controls hardware (e.g. lasers, illumination LEDs, heating elements, high-voltage stages, motors, or serial/network sockets), always emit an explicit turn-off or safe-state command during close() so the physical device is not left running unattended.
  • Always call super().close() to clean up DearPyGui tags and unregister from the module registry.
def close(self) -> None:
    # 1. Hardware safety shutdown
    if hasattr(self, "_serial_device") and self._serial_device:
        try:
            self._serial_device.write(b"SHUTDOWN_HEATER\n")
            self._serial_device.close()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"[{self.label}] Error shutting down hardware: {e}")

    # 2. Stop multiprocessing worker or background threads
    if hasattr(self, "_processor") and self._processor:
        self._processor.stop()

    # 3. Always finalize through super()
    super().close()

docs.title: 5. Receive Data via input_cb() & Validate Data Structures
docs.text:
When an upstream module sends data through a connection wire, your node's input_cb is executed.

Incoming payloads can arrive by position (args[0]) or by keyword argument (kwargs.get("data")). Always unpack both safely:

def input_cb(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    data = kwargs.get("data") if "data" in kwargs else (args[0] if args else None)
    data_type = kwargs.get("data_type", None)
    if data is None:
        return

docs.title: Important: Validate Underlying Data Structures
docs.text:
While IOTypes (e.g. IOTypes.FRAME, IOTypes.SAMPLE, IOTypes.DATALIST) identifies the semantic data contract, the underlying Python or NumPy structures can vary:

  • Image Frames: A FRAME can be 2D Grayscale (H, W), 3D BGR (H, W, 3), or 4D BGRA (H, W, 4). The data type may be np.uint8 (standard 8-bit), np.uint16 (12/16-bit HDR), or np.float32. Furthermore, upstream camera modules often wrap frames in an accessory tuple (frame, source_name).
  • Numerical Arrays: Samples or vector lists may vary in length, shape, or dimension.

Always check and validate incoming dimensions before processing:

def input_cb(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    data = kwargs.get("data") if "data" in kwargs else (args[0] if args else None)
    data_type = kwargs.get("data_type", None)
    if data is None:
        return

    # 1. Unpack accessory envelope if present
    source_name = None
    if isinstance(data, tuple) and len(data) >= 2 and isinstance(data[0], np.ndarray):
        frame, source_name = data[0], data[1]
    elif isinstance(data, np.ndarray):
        frame = data
    else:
        logger.warning(f"[{self.label}] Expected numpy array, got {type(data)}")
        return

    # 2. Check and validate matrix structure
    if frame.ndim == 2:
        # Grayscale (H, W) -> Convert to 3-channel if required by your algorithm
        frame = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)
    elif frame.ndim == 3:
        h, w, channels = frame.shape
        if channels == 4:
            frame = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGRA2BGR)
    else:
        logger.error(f"[{self.label}] Incompatible frame shape: {frame.shape}")
        return

    # 3. Proceed with processing
    self.process_frame(frame)

docs.title: 6. Send Data Downstream via trigger_cb()
docs.text:
In WindowBase, all output terminals declared in self.outputs are mapped to a connection dictionary self.connections = {terminal_name: [downstream_module, ...]}. When a user connects a wire on the canvas from output terminal_name of Node A to Node B, Node B is added to Node A's self.connections[terminal_name].

To emit data to all connected downstream modules:

class MyProducerWin(WindowBase):
    label = "Measurement Producer"

    # Declare available output terminals and their IOTypes
    outputs = {
        "Value": IOTypes.NUMBER,
        "Filtered": IOTypes.FRAME,
    }

    def emit_measurement(self, value: float) -> None:
        # Check if any modules are connected before doing heavy formatting
        targets = self.connections.get("Value", [])
        if not targets:
            return  # No downstream receivers: skip computation

        dtype = self.outputs.get("Value")
        for module in targets:
            try:
                # Downstream nodes receive the payload in input_cb
                module.input_cb(data=value, data_type=dtype)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(f"[{self.label}] Error sending to {getattr(module, 'label', 'module')}: {e}")

docs.title: 7. Zero-Wire Broadcasting (Link Bus)
docs.text:
While terminal wires are ideal for direct pipelined dataflow, drawing physical wires across the canvas for global notifications, emergency shutdowns, or cross-module synchronization can clutter the workspace.

Pipeline Creator provides link_bus (from core.link_bus import link_bus), a lightweight global Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub) event broker:

  • When to Use: Global emergency stop commands, master run/pause triggers, parameter synchronization across multiple windows, or event broadcasting.
  • Publishing: Any module can broadcast a message to a topic string.
  • Subscribing: Modules subscribe by passing a callback function.
  • Unsubscribing: Crucial! Always unsubscribe in close() to prevent memory leaks and zombie callback invocations on destroyed windows.
from core.link_bus import link_bus

class MyControllerWin(WindowBase):
    label = "Global Controller"

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

        # Subscribe to a global topic channel
        link_bus.subscribe("system/emergency_stop", self._on_emergency_stop)

    def _on_emergency_stop(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        logger.warning(f"[{self.label}] Emergency stop received!")
        self.stop_all_hardware()

    def broadcast_preset_change(self, preset_name: str) -> None:
        # Publish event to all listening modules across the application
        link_bus.publish("presets/active_preset", preset=preset_name, sender=self.UUID)

    def close(self) -> None:
        # ALWAYS unsubscribe when the module is closed or destroyed
        link_bus.unsubscribe("system/emergency_stop", self._on_emergency_stop)
        super().close()

docs.title: IOTypes Reference
docs.text:
All terminal connections use typed IOTypes. Declare what types your node accepts and emits:

from core.input_output_types import IOTypes

# In __init__:
self.accepted_input_types = [IOTypes.NUMBER, IOTypes.FRAME]
self.outputs = {
    "RESULT": IOTypes.NUMBER,
    "PREVIEW": IOTypes.FRAME,
}

Here are a few common examples of available I/O types:

# General Types
TRIGGER = ("trigger", "str or None", "Trigger event with or without attached data")
TEXT    = ("text", "str", "Standard string-based messaging")
NUMBER  = ("number", "int|float", "Numerical value for calculations or thresholds")

# Visual / Processing Types
FRAME   = ("frame", "np.ndarray or tuple(np.ndarray, str)", "8-bit image frame. Can be (frame, name).")

# Data / Control Types
CMD_DICT = ("cmd_dict", "dict", "Action command encapsulated in a dictionary")
ANY      = ("any", "Any", "Generic data type for flexible connections")

For the complete list of types, refer directly to the source file core/input_output_types.py.

docs.title: Template Files
docs.text:
Ready-to-copy starter templates are available in the template_and_doc/ folder:

template_and_doc/
├── module_template.py       ← Clean WindowBase UI module template (using self.window())
├── processor_template.py    ← Background multiprocessing worker template (ProcessingBase)
└── viewport_template.py     ← Parallel DearPyGui viewport in an isolated OS window

Use these clean templates as your starting point when creating a new module.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Pipeline Creator uses loguru as its structured logging framework. Standardized logs are formatted and printed to the terminal console, automatically written to rolling timestamped log files in the /logs directory, and captured live by the in-app Log Manager (Log Viewer window, accessible via Tools → Log Viewer), which allows operators and developers to monitor and filter events in real time by severity level.

docs.title: How to Import and Log
docs.text:
To log events from your custom modules, import logger from loguru and call the method corresponding to the desired severity level:

from loguru import logger

# TRACE: Very granular diagnostic information
logger.trace("Entering low-level computation loop")

# DEBUG: Helpful developer information
logger.debug("Applying filter matrix with size 3x3")

# INFO: General operational messages
logger.info("Camera connection initialized successfully")

# SUCCESS: Successful milestones
logger.success("CSV file successfully exported to data/output.csv")

# WARNING: Potential issues or recovery scenarios
logger.warning("Network connection latency is higher than expected")

# ERROR: Recoverable failures
logger.error("Failed to read frame from sensor, retrying...")

# CRITICAL: Fatal crashes or system instability
logger.critical("Failed to bind to communication socket. Shutting down.")

docs.title: Logging Exceptions
docs.text:
loguru has excellent support for logging exceptions with full stack traces using logger.exception():

try:
    with open("data.csv", "r") as f:
        content = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    logger.exception("Failed to load required CSV file:")

docs.title: Stress Testing & Benchmarking Your Module
docs.text:
To verify your custom module's stability, maximum throughput, queue overflow behavior, and memory footprint under heavy loads, Pipeline Creator includes a comprehensive suite of Benchmark modules located in modules/benchmark/.

Always test your module before deploying it into production pipelines:

  • As a Producer (Stress-test your module's inputs): Connect a Benchmark Producer (Video Benchmark, Sample Benchmark, Vector Benchmark, CMD Benchmark) to your module's input terminals. You can blast data at configurable frequencies (1–1000 Hz or uncapped CPU speed), testing variable payload sizes, HDR bit depths (8/12/16-bit), or waveform patterns. This allows you to evaluate your node's saturation limits, verify that your queue drop_policy (drop_oldest, drop_new, block) behaves as expected, and ensure memory remains stable.
  • As a Consumer (Stress-test your module's outputs): Connect your module's outputs to a Benchmark Processor (Image Processor Benchmark, Sample Processor Benchmark, Hardware Simulator). These mock sinks execute parameterized workloads (from zero-compute pass-through to heavy CPU/GPU matrix burns) to observe how downstream backpressure and queue delays affect your node.
  • In-Canvas Speedometer & Profiling: Pair your tests with the Propagation Tester, Flow Metrics Viewer, and in-canvas Node Profiling to measure precise transmission times (Delta-t) and queue states in real time.

For full details on the available benchmark modules and testing architecture, see Module Stress Testing & Benchmark Suite.

docs.title: Creating Documentation
docs.text: Pipeline Creator features an auto-discovery system for module documentation. When you write documentation for your custom modules, it is automatically discovered, copied, and integrated into the sidebar navigation layout when the documentation server is launched.

docs.title: How to Add Documentation to a Module
docs.text:
To write documentation for your custom module:

  1. Create a README.md file in standard Markdown format directly inside the module's subdirectory (e.g., modules/my_category/my_module/README.md).
  2. Launch or restart the local documentation server from the application menu (Help -> Documentation -> Start Server).

The documentation manager dynamically scans the /modules folder hierarchy, duplicates README.md contents into the wiki workspace, and rebuilds the navigation links under the Modules Documentation category to match your folder hierarchy.

docs.title: Fusion Manager Guide
docs.text: When working with many active modules, floating windows can clutter the workspace and overlap. The Fusion Manager is a visual layout helper that allows you to clean up your workspace by "docking" multiple independent module panels together into a single, unified window.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• 📁 Tabbed Container: Dock multiple windows into a single tabbed panel.
  • ⚙️ Quick Pipeline Rebuilding: Save and re-apply docked arrangements.
  • 🔄 Dynamic Docking/Undocking: Drag tab headers or use the manager interface to dock/undock panels on the fly.
  • 🖥️ Workspace Integration: Docked layouts are persisted when saving the workspace.

docs.title: 1. Opening the Fusion Manager
docs.text:
Ensure you are in Advanced or Dev privilege mode

  1. In the main menu bar, click Fusion Manager.
  2. Clic on Refresh to update the list of active modules.
  3. The current module will appear in the list.

docs.title: 2. Docking / Merging Modules
docs.text:
1. To dock a module into another, click and drag the source module's button from the Module column, and drop it onto the target module's button in the same column.
  2. The Merge into column will show the name of the module that the current module is merged into. It will be blank if the module is not merged into any other module.
  3. The source module will be merged into the target module, hiding the source standalone window and embedding its children inside a tab group within the target window.
  4. To restore the original state of a windows click the Restore button in the Actions column.

docs.title: 3. Nested Merging
docs.text:
Pipeline Creator supports nested merging (hierarchical docking). This means:

  • You can merge module A into module B (so A becomes a tab inside B's window).
  • You can then merge module B (which now contains A) into module C (so B and A both become tabs inside C's window).
  • This creates multi-level hierarchies, allowing you to group related tools into tabs, and then group those tab panels into larger container windows to customize your workspace as you see fit.

To build a nested hierarchy in the Fusion Manager, simply drag the button of a container module (which already has other modules merged into it) and drop it onto the button of another module.

docs.title: Main Window Guide
docs.text: The Main Window is the primary container of the application. It hosts the menu bar that gives access to all workspace management tools, visual editors, debugging utilities, and system settings.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When Pipeline Creator starts, the Main Window occupies the full viewport and acts as a top-level host for all other panels. It contains:

  1. A menu bar at the top.
  2. A transparent background canvas
  3. Modules float on top of it.

docs.title: Menu Bar
docs.text:
The active privilege mode has a direct impact on the availability and content of the different menus.

The following table summarizes all options in the menu bar along with their required privilege levels:

Option / Menu Privilege Description Workspace Advanced, Dev Allows loading and exporting pipelines or window layouts (views). Node Editor Advanced, Dev Opens the Node Editor. Fusion Manager Advanced, Dev Opens the Fusion Manager. Tools User, Advanced, Dev Access theme controls, display scaling, system debug/diagnostics panels, and the Module Manager (Advanced and Dev modes only). Help User, Advanced, Dev Access system documentation and the Tutorial Manager. Pinned User, Advanced, Dev Displays the list of currently pinned modules.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
Pipeline Creator ships with multiple color palettes. Switch between them via Tools → Theme.

Themes are defined in config/theme_colors.py as Python dictionaries. Any dictionary with an ALL_CAPS name is automatically discovered and listed as an available theme.

# Example palette definition in theme_colors.py
MY_CUSTOM_THEME = {
    "window_bg":       (20, 20, 30, 255),
    "title_bar":       (40, 40, 60, 255),
    "button":          (70, 130, 180, 255),
    "button_hover":    (100, 160, 210, 255),
    # ... more color keys
}

The active theme name is persisted in config.json under UI.theme_name and loaded on the next startup.

docs.title: Colorblind Support
docs.text:
Pipeline Creator includes colorblind-friendly palette variants. This colorization is especially helpful in the Node Editor, where data flows, individual nodes, and their corresponding windows are color-coded to make the pipeline easier to understand. These color schemes can be adjusted to suit different types of color blindness.

Set UI.colorblind_type in config.json to one of:

Value Description "none" Default palette (no adjustment) "deuteranopia" Green-blind adjusted colors "protanopia" Red-blind adjusted colors "tritanopia" Blue-blind adjusted colors

docs.title: Fusion Manager
docs.text:
The Fusion Manager is a visual helper panel that allows you to organize and clean up your workspace by combining multiple independent module panels into a single, unified tabbed window.

For more details on the layout system, see the dedicated Fusion Manager Guide.

docs.title: Accessing the Fusion Manager
docs.text:
1. Ensure the application is running in Advanced or Dev privilege mode.
  2. In the main menu bar, click Fusion Manager to open its control window.

docs.title: Drag-and-Drop Docking
docs.text: To combine floating windows: - Locate the modules you wish to combine in the Fusion Manager table. - Click and hold the module's button in the Module column. - Drag and drop it onto another module's button within the same column. - The dragged module's standalone window will automatically hide, and its controls will be embedded as a new tab inside the target module's window. - Nested Merging: Hierarchical docking is fully supported. You can merge a module into another module, and then merge that container module into a third module (e.g., merging A into B, and then B into C), creating nested, multi-level tabbed groups.

docs.title: Quick Controls
docs.text: Inside the Fusion Manager table, you can interact with the module buttons: - Left-Click a button to bring that module's window to focus. - Right-Click a button to trigger an automatic resize on that module's window.

docs.title: Undocking / Restoring Windows
docs.text: To split a module back out of a tab group: - Locate the merged module in the Fusion Manager list. - Click the Restore button in the Actions column. - The module will immediately be detached and restored as its own standalone floating window.

docs.title: Privilege Modes
docs.text:
Privilege modes control which UI features are accessible.

Whether the login screen is displayed at startup is controlled by the "Login" section in config.json: - "enabled": Set to true to display the login dialog on startup, or false to skip it. - "default_mode": Specifies the fallback privilege mode ("user", "advanced", or "dev") when the login dialog is disabled.

The login dialog can also be reopened at any time via the shortcut Ctrl + Shift + L.

When a user logs in, their username is stored in the global state container app_state.py (via the app_state.username attribute). This allows any module to retrieve the current username if needed (e.g., for user-specific logs, paths, or actions).

Mode changes automatically: - Hide/show menu items - Call update_permission() on all active module instances - Apply the mode's saved view layout

docs.title: System Tray
docs.text: When Window.minimize_to_tray is true in config.json, the Minimize to Tray menu item appears. Clicking it hides the main window and places a tray icon. Right-clicking the tray icon shows a context menu to restore or quit.

docs.title: Log Viewer
docs.text:
Pipeline Creator includes an in-app Log Viewer window that captures and displays real-time application logs. This is extremely helpful for monitoring background processes or debugging custom modules.

  • Ensure the application is running in Advanced or Dev privilege mode.
  • In the main menu bar, go to Tools and select Show Logs.

docs.title: Features of the Log Viewer
docs.text:
• Auto Scroll: Automatically scroll to the latest log entries when checked.
  • Clear View: Clear the current logs displayed in the viewer window.
  • Filter: Enter a search query to filter logs dynamically in real time.
  • Color-Coded Severity: Logs are colored based on their severity level (e.g. TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, SUCCESS, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL).

docs.title: Module Manager Guide
docs.text: The Module Manager provides a safe and visual interface to Install and Uninstall custom modules directly from the Pipeline Creator GUI.

docs.title: Installing a Module
docs.text:
The Install Module interface allows you to select a local folder, validate its contents, and copy it into the application's /modules directory.

  1. Ensure you are logged in as Advanced or Dev.
  2. Navigate to Tools → Install Module in the menu bar.

  • Browse Folder: Click the Browse... button to select a local folder containing your module.
  • Standalone Module: Check this option to install the module folder directly into the root modules/ directory (e.g., modules/my_module/).
  • Hierarchical Installation: Uncheck Standalone Module to choose a nested directory structure:
    • Parent Directory: Select an existing subdirectory inside modules/ (e.g., Camera).
    • Custom Subfolder Path: (Optional) Specify a nested subdirectory structure manually (e.g., test/rtsp), which will be created automatically.

Before allowing installation, the Module Manager runs several automated checks on the target directory:

  1. Module Presence: Verifies the folder contains at least one Python file (.py).
  2. Export Verification: Scans the Python files using static AST analysis to ensure at least one class is decorated or registered for export (e.g., defining EXPORTED_CLASS).
  3. Validation Success: Once all checks pass, the status indicator turns green, and the Install button becomes active.

docs.title: Uninstalling a Module
docs.text:
The Uninstall Module interface lists all dynamic modules installed in /modules and allows you to permanently remove them.

  1. Ensure you are logged in as Advanced or Dev.
  2. Navigate to Tools → Uninstall Module in the menu bar.

  • Hierarchical Directory Browser: Modules are displayed in a clean, collapsing folder hierarchy matching their actual location under modules/ (e.g. Camera/webcam/webcam_win).
  • Interactive Search Bar: Enter a search query to filter the tree view dynamically. The folders will automatically expand to reveal matching modules based on a fuzzy search scoring system.
  • Hover Tooltips: Hover your mouse cursor over any module button to immediately view its class description/docstring in a tooltip.
  • Visual Highlight: Clicking a module button selects it for deletion, highlighting it with a -> prefix.
  • Safety Resolution & Clean-up:
    • Shared Folders Safeguard: The uninstaller automatically compares the selected module's file path against other registered modules. If other modules share the same folder, it will only delete the selected module's specific .py file, preserving the folder and other modules.
    • Empty Parent Cleanup: If the deleted module was the last one in its folder hierarchy (e.g., in modules/test/test/), the uninstaller recursively deletes those empty parent folders up to modules/ to avoid cluttering the repository.
    • Permissions & Cache Bypass: Automatically manages read-only folder attributes and ignores locked Python __pycache__ locks under Windows to guarantee a clean and successful deletion.

docs.title: Dynamic Registry Refresh
docs.text:
Both installation and uninstallation actions automatically: 1. Re-scan the /modules folder. 2. Invalidate the global module registry cache. 3. Refresh the Node Editor search lists in real time.

You can instantly search and place your newly installed modules in the Node Editor, or verify that uninstalled modules are removed, without needing to restart the application.

docs.title: Node Editor Guide
docs.text:
The Node Editor is the central workspace of Pipeline Creator. It is a visual canvas where you import, connect, and configure node modules to build custom pipelines. These pipelines can orchestrate control flows, process data, manage hardware interactions, or run visualization routines.

  • Module Connectivity: Each module is equipped with a single input terminal and can have one or more output terminals.
  • Custom Logic: Modules can contain arbitrary code and logic. They may include a graphical user interface (GUI) window, or run entirely in the background as invisible processing units.
  • Automated Data Transfer: The link bus and wire routing system that handles data transfer between modules is completely automated by Pipeline Creator.
  • Interoperability & Future-Proofing: To ensure modules remain compatible and interoperable, a standardized Input/Output typing system validates each connection.

docs.title: Opening the Node Editor
docs.text:
1. The editor can be launched from the Main Window menu bar via Node Editor (requires Advanced or Dev privilege mode).
  2. The editor runs as a floating, resizable window within the viewport, allowing it to be moved, scaled, or docked.
  3. An infinite, pannable, and zoomable workspace where node modules are instantiated, repositioned, and linked.
  4. Right-clicking anywhere on the empty canvas opens the Module Search Popup. It allows you to search for specific modules and browse available categories (fuzzy matching supported).
  5. Hovering over any module in the search list displays its custom documentation string as a tooltip.
  6. Clicking a module from the search list instantiates the node, placing it on the canvas exactly at the current mouse pointer position.
  7. Wires can be drawn between modules by clicking and dragging from an output terminal to an input terminal. Connections can be deleted/destroyed by holding Ctrl and clicking the wire (Ctrl + Left Click).
  8. Once a module is instantiated, its corresponding control window appears. Double-clicking a module's node on the canvas brings its corresponding window to the foreground.
  9. The minimap helps you navigate and orient yourself in large, complex flow graphs.

Module Auto-Discovery & Validation

Modules are automatically detected, validated, and loaded at startup (see Developer Best Practices) from the /modules folder structure. Modules are grouped by category (their parent folder inside /modules)

Action How Pan Hold Middle Mouse Button and drag, or scroll while hovering Move node(s) Drag a selected node header Focus window Double-click a node to bring its corresponding module window to the foreground Context menu Right-click on a node to open actions: Edit Module (customize UI element visibility and layout), display module tutorial, rename the node, send to pinned modules, or delete the node/module.

Every Input/Output has a declared IOType (e.g. NUMBER, FRAME, TRIGGER, CMD_DICT). When you attempt to connect incompatible types, the editor will show a warning modal explaining the mismatch. Compatible connections are accepted silently.

docs.title: Highlighting & Dimming
docs.text:
When you select a node, Pipeline Creator highlights its downstream graph to make the data flow visible.

The highlighting mode is configurable via Node Editor → Highlight menu:

Mode Effect Show All Highlights the complete downstream chain Closest Highlights only directly connected nodes None Disables highlighting

Nodes that have no connections are dimmed to indicate they are inactive.

docs.title: Built-in Nodes: Link In / Link Out
docs.text:
These special nodes allow you to route data between modules without drawing a physical wire. Instead of a wire, they transmit data by matching channel names. This is especially useful when the output of a single module needs to feed into multiple other modules, preventing the visual workspace from being cluttered with dozens of crisscrossing wires.

Set the exact same channel name on a Link Out node and one or more Link In nodes to automatically link them.

graph LR
    A[Node A] --data--> LO[Link Out\nchannel: my_signal]
    LO -- publish --> BUS((Link Bus))
    BUS -- subscribe --> LI1[Link In\nchannel: my_signal]
    BUS -- subscribe --> LI2[Link In\nchannel: my_signal]
    LI1 --> B[Node B]
    LI2 --> C[Node C]
Clicking on a Link Out node automatically draws and highlights temporary virtual links on the canvas, allowing you to easily trace the "wireless" connections to all subscribed Link In nodes.

No IOType Validation on Virtual Wires

Unlike standard node terminals, Link In and Link Out nodes do not perform compatibility checks on IOTypes. They use the generic ANY type, which theoretically allows connecting incompatible modules.

To avoid run-time errors, it is recommended to first prototype your flow using physical wires (which validates the data types), and then replace those wires with Link In/Out nodes to clean up the canvas.

docs.title: Built-in Nodes: Gate (Conditional Flow Router)
docs.text: The Gate node acts as a switchable valve in your dataflow pipeline. It enables or stops data propagation along a branch without deleting or rewiring connections.

docs.title: Key Rules
docs.text:
• Single Input, Multiple Outputs: The In terminal accepts only 1 incoming connection to prevent collisions. The Out terminal supports multiple connections (fan-out).
  • Dynamic IOType: The gate starts as IOTypes.ANY and automatically adapts to match connected wires. Hover over In or Out to see the current type.
  • Pass-Through Toggle: Toggle the Pass checkbox directly on the node (or right-click → Toggle Pass-through). When enabled, data passes through; when disabled, data is dropped.
  • Canvas Highlighting: In highlight mode, open gates let wire highlights pass through to downstream nodes. Closed gates block highlight propagation.

Gate States in Views

Gate pass-through states (ON / OFF) are automatically preserved when exporting a View and restored upon loading. See Views & Dynamic Flow Routing.

docs.title: Edit Module UI (Module Item Inspector)
docs.text:
The Module Item Inspector allows you to inspect, declutter, and customize the user interface of any module window by selectively hiding widgets (buttons, plots, inputs).

Open it by right-clicking any node on the canvas and selecting Edit Module.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Widget Hierarchy Tree: Displays the full UI arborescence of the module. Toggle the checkbox next to any item to show or hide it.
  • Live Hover Highlighting: Hovering over an item in the tree draws a bounding overlay around that widget on the live window.
  • Interactive Pick Mode: Click Pick Element, hover over any widget on the module window, and click to automatically locate and highlight it in the tree.
  • Search & Reset: Filter widgets by tag/label using the search bar, or click Show All Elements to restore full visibility.
  • View & Flow Persistence: Hidden widget states (hidden_items) are automatically preserved when exporting Views or saving pipeline JSON files, and restored upon loading.
